title: (Scenario) How do you let an AWS Lambda in Account B use an Amazon EFS owned by Account A — why does it require solving both network connectivity (VPC peering) and authorization (EFS resource policy + Lambda execution-role EFS/VPC permissions), and why do SCPs or cross-region role assumption NOT solve it?
shortTitle: (Scenario) Cross-account AWS Lambda in Account B using Amazon EFS owned by Account A — why it needs both network connectivity and authorization, and why SCPs or cross-region role assumption do NOT solve it

s1_definition.profdef: Letting a Lambda function in Account B mount an Amazon EFS file system owned by Account A requires solving two independent problems at once. The first is network connectivity: EFS is mounted over NFS to a mount target that lives in a specific VPC and subnet, so the Lambda's VPC in Account B must have a network path to the EFS mount target's VPC in Account A, typically via VPC peering or AWS Transit Gateway, with security groups and NFS port 2049 allowed. The second is authorization: the EFS file system needs a resource policy that grants Account B's Lambda execution role permission to mount it, and that execution role needs both the EFS client permissions and the VPC networking permissions. Both must be true — a correct network path with no authorization fails, and correct authorization with no network path also fails. Service Control Policies and cross-region role assumption do not solve either problem, because SCPs can only restrict, never grant, and EFS access is a network-and-resource-policy problem, not a role-assumption problem.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Account A is the National Bank of India's central records vault building, and Account B is a partner branch that wants to read ledgers stored in that vault. Two separate things must be true for a courier from the branch to read a ledger. First, there has to be a physical road connecting the branch to the vault building — if there is no road, no amount of paperwork helps (this is the network path, VPC peering). Second, the vault's own access policy must list the branch courier as allowed to enter, and the courier must carry a pass that permits both walking the road and entering the vault (this is the EFS resource policy plus the Lambda execution role's permissions). If there is a road but the vault does not recognize the courier, entry is denied. If the vault recognizes the courier but there is no road, the courier cannot physically get there. Now, a Service Control Policy is like the bank's head office saying "no branch may EVER access any vault" — it can forbid, but it can never grant access or build a road. And cross-region role assumption is like giving the courier a pass to a vault in a different city entirely — irrelevant to reaching this vault, because EFS is reached by road and vault-policy, not by swapping identity badges.
s1_definition.oneliner: Cross-account EFS from Lambda needs BOTH a network path (VPC peering + NFS 2049) AND authorization (EFS resource policy + execution-role EFS/VPC permissions); SCPs only restrict and role assumption is the wrong tool entirely.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Letting a Lambda function in Account B mount an Amazon EFS file system owned by Account A requires solving two independent problems at once. The first is network connectivity: EFS is mounted over NFS to a mount target that lives in a specific VPC and subnet, so the Lambda's VPC in Account B must have a network path to the EFS mount target's VPC in Account A, typically via VPC peering or AWS Transit Gateway, with security groups and NFS port 2049 allowed. The second is authorization: the EFS file system needs a resource policy that grants Account B's Lambda execution role permission to mount it, and that execution role needs both the EFS client permissions and the VPC networking permissions. Both must be true — a correct network path with no authorization fails, and correct authorization with no network path also fails. Service Control Policies and cross-region role assumption do not solve either problem, because SCPs can only restrict, never grant, and EFS access is a network-and-resource-policy problem, not a role-assumption problem.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Account A is the National Bank of India's central records vault building, and Account B is a partner branch that wants to read ledgers stored in that vault. Two separate things must be true for a courier from the branch to read a ledger. First, there has to be a physical road connecting the branch to the vault building — if there is no road, no amount of paperwork helps (this is the network path, VPC peering). Second, the vault's own access policy must list the branch courier as allowed to enter, and the courier must carry a pass that permits both walking the road and entering the vault (this is the EFS resource policy plus the Lambda execution role's permissions). If there is a road but the vault does not recognize the courier, entry is denied. If the vault recognizes the courier but there is no road, the courier cannot physically get there. Now, a Service Control Policy is like the bank's head office saying "no branch may EVER access any vault" — it can forbid, but it can never grant access or build a road. And cross-region role assumption is like giving the courier a pass to a vault in a different city entirely — irrelevant to reaching this vault, because EFS is reached by road and vault-policy, not by swapping identity badges.

**One line to remember:** Cross-account EFS from Lambda needs BOTH a network path (VPC peering + NFS 2049) AND authorization (EFS resource policy + execution-role EFS/VPC permissions); SCPs only restrict and role assumption is the wrong tool entirely.

sections.s2_technical:
Amazon EFS is a network file system you reach over NFS. You do not call an EFS API to read a file; you mount the file system at an operating-system path and read it like a local disk. The mountable endpoint is an EFS mount target, and a mount target lives inside one specific VPC in one specific subnet, with an elastic network interface and a security group. This is the crucial fact: because the mount target lives in Account A's VPC, anything that wants to mount it must be able to reach that VPC's network, over TCP port 2049, which NFS uses.

A VPC-attached Lambda runs inside a VPC you configure, getting network interfaces in subnets you choose. For the Lambda in Account B to reach the EFS mount target in Account A, the two VPCs must be connected. VPC peering is the common answer: you peer Account B's VPC with Account A's VPC, add routes on both sides so traffic for the other VPC's CIDR is routed through the peering connection, and configure security groups so the EFS mount target's security group allows inbound NFS from the Lambda's security group or CIDR. Transit Gateway is the alternative when you have many VPCs. Without this network path, the mount simply times out — there is no way to reach the NFS endpoint.

Authorization is a separate axis. EFS supports a file-system resource policy, which is an IAM policy attached to the file system itself. For cross-account access, Account A attaches a resource policy to the EFS that explicitly allows Account B's Lambda execution role to perform the EFS client mount and write actions, such as `elasticfilesystem:ClientMount` and `ClientWrite`, often conditioned on a specific EFS access point. On the other side, Account B's Lambda execution role needs two sets of permissions: the EFS client actions to mount, and the VPC networking actions Lambda needs to create and manage its elastic network interfaces, which come from the AWS-managed policy for VPC access. You typically also use an EFS access point, which enforces a user identity and a root directory, so the Lambda is confined to a specific path with a specific POSIX user.

The reason both axes are mandatory is that they fail independently. If the network path is perfect but the EFS resource policy does not list Account B's role, the mount is refused with an authorization error. If the authorization is perfect but there is no peering and no route, the mount times out at the network layer. You cannot substitute one for the other — opening the network does not grant permission, and granting permission does not build the network.

Now the trap options. A Service Control Policy is an organization-level guardrail that sets the maximum permissions an account can have; it can only take permissions away, never add them. An SCP cannot grant Account B's Lambda the right to mount Account A's EFS, and it cannot create a network path — so it solves neither problem, and its only possible effect here is to accidentally block the access if written too restrictively. Cross-region role assumption is also the wrong tool: assuming a role gives you a different set of IAM credentials, but EFS mounting is not authorized by assuming a role in Account A; it is authorized by the EFS resource policy naming your execution role plus the network path. Even if the Lambda assumed a role in Account A, it would still have no network route to the mount target from its own VPC, and the mount would still time out. Region is irrelevant to this problem; mixing it in just signals a misunderstanding. The senior nuance is that EFS is fundamentally a VPC-scoped, NFS-mounted resource, so cross-account access is always a networking-plus-resource-policy exercise, never an identity-swap exercise.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, Account A is the central-records account that owns an EFS file system holding daily statement PDFs. Account B is the analytics account where Rajesh runs a Lambda that must read those PDFs to build fraud-detection features. The team keeps getting the setup wrong, so we model exactly what must be true.

Problem 1 — The first attempt gave the Lambda's execution role every EFS permission, but the mount still timed out. The reason was there was no VPC peering between Account B's VPC and Account A's VPC where the mount target lived. This is the network-connectivity half: without a route and NFS port 2049 open, authorization does not matter.

Problem 2 — The second attempt set up VPC peering correctly, but the mount was refused with an access-denied error. The reason was Account A's EFS had no resource policy allowing Account B's role, and the execution role lacked the EFS client actions. This is the authorization half.

Problem 3 — A well-meaning engineer tried to "fix" it by having the Lambda assume a role in Account A, and another tried adding an SCP. Neither worked, because role assumption does not authorize an NFS mount and an SCP can only restrict, never grant. This is the trap.

Because this is an infrastructure scenario, the mini-project models the two required conditions and the two traps as explicit checks in Java, so the logic is unambiguous and runnable. We build `EfsFileSystem` (owned by Account A, with a resource policy), `LambdaFunction` (in Account B, with a VPC and an execution role), a `NetworkPath` (peering), and an `EfsMountEvaluator` that returns whether the mount succeeds and why, plus demos showing that SCPs and cross-region assumption do not help.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run the Java demo
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/cross-account-efs-1.0.0.jar

# Real AWS equivalents (the two axes):
# AXIS 1 — network: peer the VPCs, add routes, open NFS 2049
aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-id vpc-B --peer-vpc-id vpc-A --peer-owner-id ACCOUNT_A
# (accept in Account A, add routes both sides, allow TCP 2049 in the EFS SG)

# AXIS 2 — authorization: EFS resource policy in Account A + role perms in Account B
aws efs put-file-system-policy --file-system-id fs-0abc --policy file://efs-resource-policy.json
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name fraud-lambda-exec \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an EFS `fs-0abc` owned by Account A in `vpc-A`, a Lambda `fraud-lambda` in Account B in `vpc-B` with execution role `fraud-lambda-exec`.

Step 1: Attempt 1 grants the execution role every EFS and ENI permission and adds the role to the EFS resource policy, but there is no VPC peering. The evaluator checks the network axis first, finds no route, and the mount times out. Authorization was perfect but irrelevant without a network path.

Step 2: Attempt 2 sets up peering with NFS port 2049 open, so the network axis passes, but it uses an EFS whose resource policy does not list the role. The evaluator passes the network check, then fails on the EFS resource policy, returning access denied. A network path was perfect but useless without authorization.

Step 3: The SCP trap is evaluated conceptually. An SCP can only restrict permissions, never grant them, and it cannot build a network route, so it changes nothing about the two required conditions.

Step 4: The role-assumption and cross-region trap is evaluated. Assuming a role in Account A does not authorize an NFS mount — EFS authorization comes from the resource policy naming the role plus a network path — and switching region is irrelevant because the mount target is reached by VPC route, not by region. The mount still fails.

Step 5: Attempt 3 has both axes satisfied: peering with port 2049 open, the EFS resource policy allows the role, and the execution role has both the EFS client action and the VPC ENI permissions. Every check passes and the mount succeeds.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Letting a Lambda in Account B use an EFS file system owned by Account A requires solving two completely independent problems, and the key insight is that both must be true at the same time. The first problem is network connectivity. EFS is not an API you call; it is a network file system you mount over NFS, and the mountable endpoint, the mount target, lives inside one specific VPC and subnet in Account A. So the Lambda in Account B has to be VPC-attached and its VPC must have a real network path to Account A's VPC, which in practice means VPC peering or Transit Gateway, with routes on both sides and security groups allowing NFS on TCP port 2049. The second problem is authorization. Account A must attach a resource policy to the EFS that explicitly allows Account B's Lambda execution role to mount it, and that execution role in Account B needs both the EFS client permissions like ClientMount and the VPC networking permissions Lambda needs to create its network interfaces.

The reason both axes are mandatory is that they fail independently and cannot substitute for each other. If I set up perfect authorization but there is no peering, the mount simply times out at the network layer because there is no route to the NFS endpoint. If I set up perfect peering but the EFS resource policy does not name my role, the mount is refused with an access-denied error. Opening the network does not grant permission, and granting permission does not build the network.

The two tempting wrong answers are a Service Control Policy and cross-region role assumption, and I can explain precisely why neither works. An SCP is an organization guardrail that can only restrict the maximum permissions an account has; it can never grant a permission and it certainly cannot build a network route, so it solves neither half of the problem — the only thing it could do here is accidentally block the access if written too tightly. Cross-region role assumption is simply the wrong mechanism: EFS mounting is authorized by the resource policy plus a network path, not by swapping into a role in Account A, and even if the Lambda assumed a role there it would still have no route from its own VPC to the mount target, so the mount would still time out. Region does not enter into it at all, because the mount target is reached by a VPC route, not by region.

At the National Bank of India this came up when our analytics account needed a Lambda to read statement PDFs from an EFS owned by the central-records account for fraud-detection features. The team's first attempt granted every EFS permission but the mount kept timing out, because there was no peering — pure network problem. The second attempt peered the VPCs but got access denied, because the EFS had no resource policy naming our role — pure authorization problem. Someone then tried to fix it with an SCP and someone else tried having the Lambda assume a role in the records account, and neither moved the needle for exactly the reasons I described. It only worked once we had both: VPC peering with port 2049 open, and the EFS resource policy allowing our execution role, which itself had the EFS client actions plus the VPC access permissions. That experience is why I always frame cross-account EFS as a networking-plus-resource-policy exercise, never an identity-swap exercise.
